props.title: The Cat Concerto

sections.content: The Cat Concerto (1947) stands as one of MGM's finest Tom and Jerry shorts, masterfully blending classical music with slapstick comedy. The cartoon's use of Franz Liszt's "Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2" follows a proud tradition started by Rhapsody Rabbit (1946) featuring Bugs Bunny and The Mouse Concerto (1946) with Mickey Mouse. This seven-minute masterpiece showcases Tom as a concert pianist whose performance is repeatedly disrupted by Jerry, who's been sleeping inside the piano. The precision timing of the animation to Liszt's complex musical piece set new standards for musical animation.

sections.content: The influence of The Cat Concerto rippled through animation history. Its sophisticated integration of classical music with physical comedy inspired countless cartoons, including What's Opera, Doc? (1957), which similarly elevated cartoon slapstick through classical music. The short's attention to musical timing and gesture animation became a blueprint for animating musical performances, evident in films like Allegro Non Troppo (1976) and segments of Fantasia 2000 (1999).

The technical achievement of synchronizing animation to classical music in The Cat Concerto deserves special attention. Directors William Hanna and Joseph Barbera, along with animator Kenneth Muse, created precise frame-by-frame animations matching every note of Liszt's composition. This meticulous approach influenced later musical animations like Pink Floyd – The Wall (1982) and Peter and the Wolf (2006). SUBHEAD: Musical Animation Legacy

sections.content: The marriage of classical music and animation reached new heights following The Cat Concerto. Modern films like Coco (2017) and Soul (2020) continue this tradition of precise musical animation, though with contemporary compositions. The short's influence can be seen in sequences like the piano scene in Corpse Bride (2005) and the orchestra segments in Amadeus (1984), where music drives both narrative and visual rhythm.
